questions.question: A support lead argues for building a feature on the strength of three customer requests that all arrived through one account manager. The leader replies: "Three requests through one channel is not prevalence — go test the underlying claim first." What is the cost of this response?
options: None; the advice is accurate and saves a wasted cycle
It is correct advice that produces dependence — the next recommendation will also arrive unexamined, waiting for the leader to find the gap
It is too harsh and will discourage the support lead from bringing signals forward
It confuses evidence quality with prioritization, which are separate questions
questions.explanation: The advice is right, which is what makes it the expensive failure. A is the tempting answer because accuracy feels like sufficiency; but the person learns the leader's conclusion, not how to reach one, and returns next month with the same unexamined shape. C misreads the problem as tone.

questions.question: Which of these is a calibrated coaching question rather than a verdict in question form?
options: "Do you really think three requests count as a pattern?"
"Wouldn't you agree we should test this before we commit a cycle?"
"Walk me through how each of these three requests reached us. What was the path?"
"What is the true prevalence of this problem across all enterprise leads?"
questions.explanation: C is answerable from what the person already holds, has probably not been examined, and cannot be answered without exposing the single-channel problem. A and B are verdicts with question marks. D is the tempting one — it sounds rigorous and points at the real gap, but there is no path to an answer this week, so it produces paralysis rather than thinking.

questions.question: A PM presents a decision. The leader thinks the reasoning has a hole but wants to keep ownership with the PM. Which response best preserves ownership?
options: "Let's work through it together in our one-to-one and land on something we're both happy with"
"Your evidence section does not say who you did not hear from. What would tell you they disagreed?"
"I'd probably go the other way on this, but it's your call"
"Send it to me and I'll add the missing analysis so we can move quickly"
questions.explanation: B names the missing exposure without naming a preferred conclusion, so the PM does the work. A and D are the phase's recurring trap — both sound supportive and both quietly relocate the decision to the leader. C is more subtle: stating a preferred answer while calling it their choice makes the rest of the conversation about pleasing the leader.

questions.question: A decision must be made today, and the person holding it cannot close the evidence gap in time. What does the model say?
options: Coach anyway; the deadline is less important than the development
Approve their current reasoning to preserve their ownership
Extend the deadline, since a decision made without the evidence is not worth making
Give the answer, and label it — say you are deciding this one, and name the question you would have asked
questions.explanation: This is the boundary of the model. Coaching costs more per decision and pays back only when the class recurs and there is time to close the gap. A is tempting because development sounds like the higher value, but coaching someone into a deadline they will miss is not development. Labelling the takeback is what keeps it instructive rather than corrosive.

questions.question: After eight weeks of coaching, which observation best indicates that judgment has actually transferred?
options: The person's recommendations are better written and better evidenced than before
The person agrees with the leader's assessment more often than they used to
The person now arrives with the weakest exposure in their own case already named and addressed
The person escalates fewer decisions and acts more independently
questions.explanation: The test is whether the gap gets found before it reaches you. A is the tempting distractor: output quality can improve purely because the person learned which boxes you check, which is compliance. B measures convergence on your taste. D can equally mean they have stopped surfacing things you should see.
